opus-5.5.text:
I think they're coming at it from quite different starting points, and that difference matters.

Google, especially through DeepMind, has been doing AI for Science for close to a decade now, and their style is very much "pick a hard, well-defined scientific problem and build a specialized system to crack it." AlphaFold is the iconic example. Protein structure prediction had a clear benchmark, decades of curated data in the Protein Data Bank, and a community that agreed on what success looked like. DeepMind went deep, built a purpose-designed architecture, and delivered something that changed structural biology. They've repeated that playbook with materials discovery, weather forecasting, and mathematics. It's a very scientist-driven, problem-first approach, and it produces results that the scientific community can immediately verify and use.

OpenAI's approach is more "general model first, science as an application." Their bet is that if you make the foundation model capable enough at reasoning, coding, reading literature, and planning, it becomes a kind of universal research assistant, or eventually a research collaborator. So instead of building an AlphaFold for every domain, they're asking: can one model help a chemist, a physicist, and a biologist all at once, by reasoning through problems, writing analysis code, and proposing hypotheses? That's a much broader ambition, and it scales across fields, but the outputs are harder to validate. A predicted protein structure can be checked against an experiment. A model's "insight" in a research conversation is much fuzzier.

Personally, I don't see them as opposing strategies so much as two layers that will eventually merge. The specialized models are like very precise instruments, a microscope or a telescope. The general models are more like the researcher who knows how to use all the instruments. The most interesting systems going forward will probably be agents built on general models that can call specialized tools, run simulations, maybe even drive automated labs, and then reason over the results.

The real bottleneck, for both, is not the model. It's data and experimental feedback. In many scientific fields, the data is scarce, noisy, or locked up, and the only way to know whether a hypothesis is right is to go do the experiment, which is slow and expensive. Whoever figures out how to close that loop, connecting AI to real-world experimentation at scale, is going to have the biggest impact. Google has a head start in deep domain partnerships and scientific credibility; OpenAI has momentum in general reasoning capability and a huge user base of researchers already using its models every day. I think both will matter, and honestly the scientific community benefits from having both philosophies being pushed hard at the same time.

fable-5.1.text:
I think the two companies are coming at this from very different places, and that shapes everything.

Google, through DeepMind, has been doing AI for Science for a long time, and the AlphaFold lineage is the clearest example. Their approach is very much "pick a well-defined scientific problem with a clean benchmark, build a specialized model, and win decisively." Protein structure, weather forecasting, materials discovery with GNoME, fusion plasma control, math olympiad problems with AlphaProof and AlphaGeometry. Each of these is a domain where you can measure progress rigorously, and they have deep in-house scientific talent plus the compute and patience to go after them. The strength is that the results are real and verifiable. The weakness, if you want to call it that, is that each of these is a bespoke effort. AlphaFold doesn't help you with weather. It's a portfolio of brilliant point solutions rather than a general scientific engine.

OpenAI is almost the opposite. They have essentially bet that the path to AI for Science runs through general reasoning models. The idea is that if you make a model good enough at math, coding, and long-horizon reasoning, it will become a useful scientific collaborator across domains without you building a dedicated system for each one. You see this in how they talk about the o-series and the reasoning models, and in things like the FrontierMath results or their work with national labs. Their framing is less "we solved protein folding" and more "we built something that can help a physicist think."

My honest view is that both are necessary and they're converging. Google is increasingly layering general models on top of their specialized tools, and OpenAI is increasingly realizing that general reasoning alone doesn't get you to a validated scientific result. You still need the experimental loop, the domain data, the verification. The companies that eventually do this well will probably look like a hybrid: a general reasoning layer that knows when to call out to specialized, physics-grounded models, and a tight connection to actual labs so that hypotheses get tested rather than just generated.

The thing I'd push back on in the current discourse is the idea that a model producing plausible-sounding hypotheses is the same as doing science. Science is mostly about being wrong efficiently. Right now Google's approach produces fewer but more trustworthy wins, and OpenAI's produces more breadth but more that needs checking. Neither has fully closed the loop yet, and that closing of the loop is where I think the real competition will be over the next couple of years.

astra-6.text:
I’d look at two things: how AI helps scientists do research, and how it helps them solve a particular scientific problem. Those are related, but they’re not quite the same.

One approach is to build a system around a specific problem, incorporating the constraints of that field and evaluating it against scientific results. Another is to build a general-purpose model that helps across the research process—from reading papers and writing code to proposing explanations and designing experiments.

That’s the distinction I’d use to assess Google and OpenAI, although I wouldn’t draw a rigid line between them or claim to know their internal priorities. A specialized system can produce a substantial advance in one area, while a general system can make many researchers more productive. Neither automatically guarantees scientific discovery.

For me, the decisive question is whether the output survives validation. Can you test the prediction? Can you reproduce the result? Does it tell you something you didn’t already know? Generating a plausible hypothesis is useful, but the scientific value comes from closing that loop with evidence.

sol-6.1.text:
I’d distinguish them by where they put their emphasis. Google’s approach has been more visibly organized around specific scientific problems: use AI to tackle a problem in biology, chemistry, or another discipline, and evaluate progress against that field’s standards. OpenAI’s emphasis has been on building general-purpose models that could help across many kinds of scientific work, from reading papers and writing code to reasoning through a hypothesis.

Those approaches are complementary. A specialized model can make a major contribution to one well-defined problem, while a general-purpose model can help connect the steps in a researcher’s workflow. But neither approach should be judged only by how impressive its answers sound. For science, the question is whether it produces reliable predictions, useful experiments, and results that other researchers can reproduce. That connection to experimental validation is where I’d focus when assessing either company.
